extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 5, printed three days after the scene date — so its advertising is the closest the American gets to describing the town of 1835-07-01. Three placements the run has been chasing land here: Tuthill King's clothing store is three doors north of the TREMONT HOUSE in Dearborn street, Rockwell's furniture stand is on SOUTH Water street at the stand formerly occupied by Clark & Co., and Henry Moore keeps his law office in J. H. Kinzie's new building. It also contradicts itself and the two issues before it about which Water street the forwarding houses stand in, which this file records rather than resolves.

claims.notes: A NAMED BUILDING WITH A NAMED TENANT: 'Office at J. H. Kinzie's New [Building]'. J. H. Kinzie is the merchant and steamboat agent this run has already documented three times over, and he has a NEW building in July 1835 with a lawyer in it — a documented first-floor-and-above use this project's commercial frontage has had no instance of. THE WORD AFTER 'New' IS CUT ('New lon') and 'Building' is bracketed as a supply; 'Block' and 'Row' are equally consistent with the fragment and none of them changes the claim, which is that Kinzie put up a new building and let office space in it. NO STREET: the card does not say where the building is, so the placement is `relative` on the building and the street is null. The reference to Joseph Story of Cambridge is quoted as printed and is not treated as a Chicago person.

claims.notes: THREE FORWARDING HOUSES IN ONE COLUMN, AND THE RUN NOW CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT WHICH WATER STREET TWO OF THEM STAND IN. On 1835-06-20 page 3 column 6 the same two cards print 'NORTH WATER STRERT' (Sabine, line 346) and 'NORTH WaTEM sTRERT' (John Davi[s], line 360), both legible enough that the word is not in doubt. Here the same two print 'OUTH WATER STREET' and 'DUTH WATER STREET', where the first letter is cut and 'OUTH' can only be SOUTH. So either the firms moved across the river between 20 June and 4 July, or one printing is a compositor's or the OCR's error. THIS FILE DOES NOT DECIDE IT. The street is recorded on John Davis's entity as South Water Street from what THIS issue prints, the earlier claims keep North from what THEY print, and the gazetteer will therefore show him associated with both — which is the honest state of the evidence and exactly what a reader needs to see before putting a warehouse on a bank. Newberry & Dole's card gives no street in any printing. THE SURNAME 'DAVIS' IS COMPLETE HERE for the first time, where 1835-06-13 and 06-20 both cut it after 'DAVE'/'DAVIK' and no completion was made; this printing is what settles it.

This printing sets 'fremont House' with only the initial cut, and Tremont is the only reading. So Tuthill King's New York Clothing Store stands in Dearborn Street, three doors north of the Tremont House — an offset, a direction, a street and a named anchor, which is the strongest placement in the run and the only one with all four. claims.notes: THE FOURTH PRINTING OF ROCKWELL'S CARD IS THE ONE THAT PLACES HIM. Three issues cut the sentence in three different places; this one carries it whole enough to read 'at the stand on S[outh] Water street, formerly occupied by Clark, [?] Co.' — a succession placement, which is the strongest kind this corpus can give because it names the tenancy the shop replaced. It agrees with 1835-06-27's land notice directing applicants to 'ROCKWELL, South Water street', so two independent advertisements now put him on the same street. THE PREDECESSOR IS HALF-READ: 'Clark, Fils Go.' has a surname and then something that is not resolvable — 'Fils' is not an English firm word and 'Go.' is 'Co.', so the firm is Clark and at least one partner. Left inside `[uncertain: …]`. The full furniture list is quoted here for the first time and is the most detailed interior-goods evidence in the run.

claims.notes: THE CROSS-EXAMINATION THIS TICKET EXISTS FOR, AND IT LANDS ON THE PROJECT'S OWN FIXTURE. T-0257's worked fixture reads a South Water Street advertisement in the Democrat of the scene date signed 'J. S. C. HOGA[N]', standing 'one [door from] the Post Office'; the same issue carries a post-office notice signed only 'HOGAN, P. M.', and the fixture explicitly REFUSED to say the merchant and the postmaster were one man, noting that a merge would have to be declared. The American settles it two days later: this notice is signed with the FULL initials, 'J. S. C. HOGAN, Postmaster'. The gazetteer keys persons on the whole normalized name, so the two coalesce here with no merge rule needed and none is written — the identification is carried by the evidence, not by a declaration, which is the case the identity policy was designed to allow. WHAT ELSE THIS PUTS ON THE MAP: the post office keeps posted hours and opens on Sundays after a mail, and the Democrat places Hogan's store one door from it on South Water Street — so the post office is a South Water Street tenancy at the scene date. THE HOURS THEMSELVES ARE CUT: the figures before 'o'clock A.M.' are destroyed and are not supplied.

claims.notes: THE PORT OF CHICAGO ACROSS THE SCENE DATE ITSELF — arrivals from June 27 to July 3 and clearances on July 1. What was in the river on 1835-07-01: the schooner Philips clearing for Milwaukee and the Jesse Smith clearing the same day, and in the days either side of it the Llewelling twice, the Hiram from Michigan with LUMBER, the Jesse Smith from Green Bay with LUMBER, the Whig with merchandize, the brig Neptune with POTATOES and the steamboat Michigan outbound. Two lumber cargoes in one week is the useful number: this project builds a town of sawn boards and can now say where they came in and how often. THE DESTINATION COLUMN IS CUT down the right edge throughout and no route is completed that the transcription does not carry; the master of the Philips is 'Howe' inbound and 'Lows' outbound on consecutive lines, read as one man and bracketed.

claims.notes: A DWELLING PLACED AGAINST THE PUBLIC SQUARE, dated the scene week — and the Public Square is ground this project models and has argued about for months with almost no documentary frontage evidence. The address gives THREE things at once: the square, Monroe Street, and 'west of' something whose name is cut away. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the word before 'Public Square' reads 'sou' and is left inside `[uncertain: …]` — 'south of the Public Square' and 'on the south side of the Public Square' place a house differently, and the difference matters at this scale. THE SURNAME is cut after 'MOR' and completed to More; Moore is equally consistent, and this issue separately carries an attorney 'HUNKY MOOR)' — Henry Moore — with an office in J. H. Kinzie's new building, so the two are NOT identified with each other: different forenames, different addresses, and same-surname-different-initials is the one merge this project never makes.

claims.notes: FOUR ADVERTISEMENTS THE PREVIOUS ISSUE COULD ONLY HALF-READ, FINISHED HERE, and they are quoted together because the segmenter runs them into two lines. THE LIVERY'S SECOND PARTNER is J. N. Story, a single letter on 1835-06-27. THE AUCTIONEER is W. Montgomery, and his room is the STORE OF D[?] CARVER, some doors west of J. Wright's on South Water Street — a succession placement with a named predecessor and a named neighbour, which is as good as this corpus gets; the number of doors and Carver's forename are both cut. HIS FIRST SALE IS ON THE SCENE DATE: 'Wednesday the 1st day of July' — 1835-07-01 was a Wednesday, which resolves the ambiguity 1835-06-27's claim left open between the 1st and the last day of the month, and it means an auction of merchandize, real estate and town lots was being held on South Water Street on the day this project reconstructs.
